subject: if Distance gives bias estimates when transects are shortened

messages.author: d83f73a3df929863
messages.subject: if Distance gives bias estimates when transects are shortened
parts:
Hello

=20

We counted the numbers of birds seen in an area of sea from a low flying
aircraft, flying along parallel line transects, using standard JNCC
aerial survey methods. The raw data were processed through Distance to
estimate the total number of birds in the entire survey area. =20
=20
We then selected a subsection of the area of search, selecting areas of
higher density. We want to estimate the numbers of birds within the
higher density subsection. =20
=20
If we use Distance, we are deliberately shortening transects to exclude
sections of transects where no or few birds were seen, with the result
that our estimate of numbers of birds within the higher density area is
similar or sometimes greater than in the total area of search. Eric, in
a correspondence dated 9 April, you say, "Transect length needs to
accurately reflect the amount of effort expended in the survey. I worry
that you might adjust transect length to remove sections of transect
where effort was expended but nothing was seen. That would badly bias
the estimated density or abundance."
=20
If distance is not a suitable method for estimating the numbers of birds
within the higher density area, do you have any suggestions for
alternative methods?
=20
Thanks in advance for your help
=20
Sue

=20

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: if Distance gives bias estimates when transects are shortened
parts:
Sue, data-dependent post-stratification of this type is prone to bias.
This isn't something specific to Distance. However, if you're in the
situation that there really aren't any birds in the areas where none
were detected, and almost all the birds are within the region you've
identified from the data, bias is likely to be small. Note though that
even if bias in quantifying what was there at the time of the survey is
small, many of those birds might be outside that small area next day -
or even later the same day.

Depending on how clustered the distribution is, you might want to
consider using Distance to fit density surface models - and you can
estimate numbers in any sub-area of interest by integrating under the
parts of that surface corresponding to the sub-area.

Steve Buckland
